title: Arlo and the Missing Banister
markdown:
The Atherton Museum buzzed toward its first late opening. Arlo, fox archivist, glasses that missed nothing, tweed waistcoat buttoned over nervous energy, was in charge. His ambition: a flawless evening, free of his friend Edie’s overwhelming shine.

Edie the pine marten, bushy tail matching her spirit, adored him. “Point me to anything, and I will make it shine!”

He saw a chance to keep her busy and set a pact, kind and strict: polish the grand staircase banister until it gleamed unequivocally, like a looking-glass. The condition, so obvious he did not say it, was that a banister belongs on stairs.

The brass itself was an enchanted companion of a sort: cold, scrolled, smelling of old polish and a hundred hands, catching lantern-light in a river of small suns. Edie darted off with a rustle. Arlo already suspected gleam would be an understatement.

Twilight. Lanterns warm. His gaze found the staircase and two plain wooden posts. The banister was gone. Panic gnawed. Nearby, Edie, paws smudged metallic, held a curving section of ornate brass, triumphant.

“Edie. What have you done?”

“I polished it, Arlo! Just as you said! I took it right off to reach every inch. Perfect! Better than my bedroom mirror!”

Taboo broken: the looking-glass had left the stairs.

First guests: a distinguished owl tilting his head; sparrows chirping bewilderment; formidable Mrs Higgins the headmistress stopping short. The entrance looked incomplete.

Heat climbed Arlo’s neck. He looked at Edie’s innocent triumph.

Three awkward tasks, solved by kindness rather than scolding. He walked back, weary smile. “Edie. A banister, while needing a brilliant polish, is generally more effective attached to the stairs.”

Her spark flickered, then reignited. “Oh. Oh dear. That makes a lot of sense, doesn’t it?”

A shared quiet chuckle. He patted her shoulder. “We will sort this. Together.”

They propped the gleaming curve against a pedestal: an impromptu sculpture, the beast’s true form for one night. Velvet-roped stanchions closed the gaps. They guided guests past the unconventional entrance. Awkwardness dissolved; Arlo’s self-deprecating explanations charmed. Whispers became laughter. Mrs Higgins even circled the brass as if it were a loan from a modern wing.

Evening closed. Arlo sat beside Edie. “I was so convinced I had to do this alone. Worried about not being rescued. Sometimes the best solutions are born from admitting you need help. Or, at least, sensible re-attachment.”

Edie nudged him. “And sometimes a very shiny banister can be more art exhibit than staircase.”

He chuckled, light, free. Not archival perfection: a success, friendship stronger. Brass polish mingled with amused echoes. Loyalty, it turned out, was keeping the promise to shine and the promise to stay, even when the looking-glass had wandered off the stairs.
